caption:
Ever press a fingernail into a bug bite to make the itch stop? There’s actually a physiological explanation to this called gate control.

When the skin is pressed, touch and pain fibers fire and tell the spinal cord to block the itch signal before it reaches the brain. Interestingly, pressing about one centimeter beside the bite blocks the itch more effectively than pressing directly on it.

But, there’s a caveat. The itch relief fades in thirty to sixty seconds, and repeated pressing or scratching can break the skin and open the door to infection, or restart the itch scratch cycle entirely.

Thankfully, topical hydrocortisone or antihistamines, oral antihistamines and cold compresses all interrupt itch through more durable pathways.

It’s important to remember that if a bite becomes increasingly swollen, spreads, or comes with fever, that is no longer simple itch and needs medical attention rather than a home remedy.

So yes, the nail trick has real neuroscience behind it. But if lasting relief is the goal, there are better tools for the job.

BREAKING: Alberta has just issued a West Nile virus warning after record rain triggered a mosquito boom across the province. Here’s what you actually need to know.

Most people bitten by an infected mosquito never get sick. About 1 in 5 develop symptoms. The vast majority of those are mild: fever, headache, body aches, fatigue, sometimes a rash. This resolves on its own with rest and fluids, usually within a week or two.

A much smaller number, less than 1%, develop severe neurological illness: encephalitis or meningitis, meaning inflammation of the brain or spinal cord. This is where West Nile becomes dangerous. Risk of severe disease increases with age, and there is no specific treatment or antiviral for West Nile virus. Care is supportive.

When to go to the ER:
• A severe headache unlike any you’ve had before
• High fever that isn’t breaking
• Confusion or difficulty staying alert
• Stiff neck
• New muscle weakness or paralysis
• A seizure

These are signs of possible neuroinvasive disease and need to be assessed immediately, not managed at home.

Risk is highest early July through the first hard frost. Here’s how to protect yourself:
• Cover up at dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active. Long sleeves, long pants, light colours.
• Use a Health Canada registered repellent. DEET is not recommended for infants under six months. For kids six months to two years, limit to once daily use. Over two years, up to three times a day is fine. 
• Empty standing water around your home. Forgotten watering cans, bird baths, clogged gutters. These are mosquito nurseries.
• Make sure window and door screens are intact.

Most people who get bitten will be completely fine. But knowing the red flags means you’re not guessing if something feels off.

Sources: Primary Care Alberta, Alberta Health Services

BREAKING: Cyclospora Outbreak declared in the United States. 

CDC’s official surveillance count is 145 cases across 17 states, tracked between May 1 and June 16. Since then, Michigan has reported its own rapidly growing cluster (close to 700 cases as of July 6, about 13.5 times their typical yearly total), which puts the national number well past 450 and likely still rising.

A few things worth knowing if you or someone in your life develops symptoms:
- Standard stool cultures and many routine diarrhea panels do not test for Cyclospora. You need to specifically request it, usually via PCR or special staining.
- Symptoms can take one to two weeks to show up after exposure, so it can be hard to trace back to a specific meal.
- It is not spread person to person, so no need to isolate from family, but anyone symptomatic and preparing food for others should be diligent with handwashing.
- Treatment is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. If you have a sulfa allergy, talk to your doctor about alternatives, since options are less well studied.
- No food recall has been issued yet. Investigators in Michigan and federally have not pinpointed a single confirmed source yet, though contaminated fresh produce is the leading hypothesis based on past outbreaks.
- washing doesn’t reliably remove the parasite, but it’s still recommended to wash your produce thoroughly to reduce risk

If you’ve had diarrhea lasting more than a few days, especially if it’s watery and comes with fatigue or cramping, it’s worth a conversation with your doctor and specifically naming Cyclospora as something you want ruled out.

Source: CDC Cyclosporiasis Surveillance, Michigan Dept of Health and Human Services, Ohio Department of Health.

caption:
Most rashes can wait for an appointment, but this is one that shouldn’t. 

A painful, blistering rash on the tip of your nose can be a warning sign that shingles is affecting the nerve that also supplies your eye. This is called Hutchinson’s sign, and it increases the risk of eye involvement, which can lead to permanent vision impairment if not recognized and treated promptly.

Thankfully, early treatment is effective. Antiviral medication works best when started within the first 72 hours of the rash appearing, and if your eye is involved, you’ll likely need urgent assessment by an ophthalmologist.

One important point: Hutchinson’s sign is a warning sign, not a guarantee. Some people with shingles on the tip of the nose never develop eye complications, while others can have serious eye involvement without a rash on the nose. That’s why any shingles rash on the forehead, around the eye, or on the nose, especially if accompanied by eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, or changes in vision, should be assessed urgently.

Shingles is preventable. Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of developing shingles and its complications and is recommended for many older adults and others at increased risk.

caption:
Mosquito season is here and your scratching is making it worse. Here’s what actually works.

1. Cool compress
Apply a cold pack or cloth for 10 minutes at a time. This constricts blood vessels, reduces swelling and gives you temporary itch relief without any medication. Safe for all ages. Do this first before reaching for anything else.

2. Calamine lotion
The pink stuff your mom used actually holds up. It contains zinc oxide, which soothes itching and helps dry out any weeping skin. Apply directly to the bite a few times a day. Safe for children over 2. Avoid getting it near eyes or mouth.

3. Topical antihistamines
Creams like diphenhydramine (Benadryl cream) block the histamine response right at the bite. Apply a thin layer up to 3-4 times daily. Generally not recommended for children under 2 without a doctor’s guidance, and avoid using on broken or infected skin.

4. Oral antihistamines
When a bite is driving you absolutely mad or you have multiple, a systemic antihistamine like cetirizine (Reactine) or loratadine (Claritin) works from the inside out. Non-drowsy options are safe for most adults and children over 2 at age-appropriate doses. Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) works well but will make you drowsy. Always check with your doctor or pharmacist first. 

5. Topical steroids
A low-potency hydrocortisone cream (0.5-1%) is one of the most effective options for reducing inflammation and itch. Apply a thin layer 1-2 times daily for no more than 7 days. Not recommended for children under 2 without medical advice. Avoid applying to the face, groin or underarms.

What not to do:
• Do not scratch. It breaks the skin, introduces bacteria and triggers more histamine release, making the itch worse.
• Do not apply toothpaste, butter or essential oils. No evidence. Some cause skin irritation.
• Do not use topical antibiotics prophylactically on an uninfected bite.

See a doctor if:
• there is increasing warmth or redness 
• fever, swollen lymph nodes or flu like symptoms 
• signs of a severe allergic reaction
• bite is not improving after a week 
• you’re worried and something doesn’t seem right

The hardest part about spotting misinformation is that there isn’t a giant warning label attached to it.

In fact, some of the most misleading health content online can look very credible. I was recently part of a panel with @albertabluecross discussing women’s health and misinformation. A few key takeaways are below. 

COMMENT “PANEL” for the link to the full discussion. 

A few red flags to watch for:
• It promises a simple solution to a complex problem
• It relies heavily on personal testimonials instead of scientific evidence
• It describes a treatment as being “suppressed,” “hidden” or something “doctors don’t want you to know.”
• It cherry-picks a single study while ignoring the broader body of evidence
• It encourages you to distrust every expert, institution or source of information except the person making the claim
• It uses fear, outrage or urgency to push you toward a decision
• It sounds too good to be true

None of these automatically mean a claim is false, but they should make you pause and ask a few more questions before accepting it as fact.

The reality is that science is often nuanced. It evolves over time. And it rarely deals in absolutes. That uncertainty can feel uncomfortable, but it’s actually one of the things that makes science trustworthy.

caption:
Canadian Summers mean both sunscreen AND bug spray together. Turns out, the order AND the type of bug spray matter.

Here’s the deal:
1. Apply sunscreen FIRST, wait 15–30 min, then bug spray on top

2. DEET (the most common repellent) reduces your sunscreen’s SPF by about a THIRD

3. Picaridin/Icaridin works just as well as DEET but does NOT reduce your sunscreen’s protection, making it the better choice when you’re layering both

4. If you do use DEET, reapply sunscreen more often and add UPF clothing or a hat

5. Skip combo sunscreen + bug spray products. They don’t work well because sunscreen and repellent have different reapplication schedules

TL;DR: Sunscreen first. Bug spray second. Pick picaridin when you can.

The patient with uncontrolled diabetes who stopped taking insulin. The patient with heart failure who stretched out their pills to make them last longer. The patient whose blood pressure medication ran out weeks ago.

Natural Mosquito Repellents: What Does the Science Say?

With so many “natural” bug sprays on the market, here’s what the research actually shows about three popular plant-based options and why the synthetics still come out on top.

SATSUMA (Citrus reticulata)

Satsuma peel oil contains limonene and other compounds that have shown mosquito-repellent and larvicidal activity in lab studies. In fact, mandarin oil was the most active fumigant against adult mosquitoes among citrus species tested. However, the effect is short-lived due to the volatile nature of the oils, and there is no evidence supporting satsuma as a reliable personal repellent in real-world conditions.

OIL OF LEMON EUCALYPTUS (OLE / PMD)

OLE is the gold standard of natural repellents. It’s the only plant-derived option recommended by the CDC alongside synthetic repellents. Its active ingredient, PMD (para-menthane-3,8-diol), can provide 2–6 hours of protection and has shown efficacy comparable to DEET in some studies. Important: OLE should NOT be used on children under 3 years old, and it is classified as an eye irritant.

CITRONELLA

Despite its popularity, citronella offers significantly shorter protection than DEET. One study found just 10.5 minutes of complete protection vs. 360 minutes for DEET. Some countries (including Canada and in Europe) have restricted citronella-based repellents due to concerns about methyl eugenol, a component classified as possibly carcinogenic.

THE BOTTOM LINE

If you’re in an area with mosquito-borne diseases like malaria, dengue, or Zika, DEET and picaridin (also known as icaridin) remain the most effective and longest-lasting repellents (providing 5–9+ hours of reliable protection). They are the first-line recommendations from the CDC and WHO for disease prevention.

Natural options like OLE can be a reasonable alternative for lower-risk settings, but they require more frequent reapplication and are not substitutes for DEET or picaridin when it matters most.

With semaglutide recently becoming available as a generic medication in Canada, I’ve been seeing a lot of questions about whether generic medications are “just as good” as brand name drugs.

Many people assume that because generics cost less, they must be lower quality.

Generic medications actually contain the same active ingredient as the brand name version and must meet strict standards for safety, quality and effectiveness. Before they’re approved, manufacturers have to demonstrate that the medication performs similarly in the body to the original product.

The biggest differences are usually things like the name, colour, shape, packaging or inactive ingredients.

This means that for most medications and most patients, a generic version works just as well as the brand name version. I buy almost exclusively generic medications for myself and my family when they’re available. 

There are some exceptions. A small number of people may react differently to fillers or dyes, and there are a handful of medications where even small differences in absorption can be important. That’s why it’s always worth discussing any concerns with your pharmacist or healthcare professional.

There’s a much bigger story here…generic medications help improve access, reduce costs and make important treatments available to more people.

Generic doesn’t mean “inferior.” It usually means the patent expired.

caption:
How many times have you been worried about an infected bug bite?

One day it’s a simple mosquito bite. By the next morning the skin around it is swollen, red and hot to the touch. Though many may confuse this for an infection, it’s actually something called skeeter syndrome. It’s a local reaction to proteins in mosquito saliva.

The main clue is that it shows up fast, usually within hours of the bite. Infections build slowly over a day or two. Skeeter syndrome, on the other hand, hits early and hits big, often much larger than you’d expect from one bite.

It’s more common in young kids but it can occur in adults too, especially if you or your child have a history of eczema or other allergies. Once you react this way, you’re likely to react this way again with future bites.

Thankfully, most cases settle with an antihistamine, a cool compress and elevation. No antibiotics needed.

It’s important to see a doctor if you have:
- Redness that keeps spreading past 48 hours 
- Red streaking away from the bite 
- Fever 
- You feel unwell or the pain is worsening 
- Swelling near the eye or affecting breathing or swallowing 
- You’re unsure if it’s a local reaction or infected

Of course, when in doubt, get it looked at. A hot swollen patch of skin can look identical whether it’s your immune system overreacting or a true infection starting, so it’s always best to err on the side of caution.

• Plan outdoor activities for the early morning or evening whenever possible

• Take frequent breaks in air-conditioned spaces or the shade
• Use fans, cool showers, misting or cool compresses to help lower your body temperature

Studies show that people with Type O blood can attract nearly TWICE as many mosquito landings as Type A — but it also depends on the mosquito species. Some prefer Type B!

But blood type is only part of the puzzle. The biggest factor? Your skin chemistry. People who are “mosquito magnets” produce higher levels of certain fatty acids on their skin — and that difference can last for YEARS.
Bottom line: your blood type matters, your skin matters more, and either way wear repellent and long clothing.

caption:
Is a full body scan the smartest way to catch cancer early?

Whole body MRI screening is being sold as peace of mind for healthy adults. Though many may confuse this for a modern upgrade to cancer screening, it’s actually a test with almost no evidence behind it for people without symptoms or risk factors.

In recent screening data, the vast majority of scans turned up a finding of some kind, but very few of those findings were cancer. The rest led to more imaging, more biopsies and more anxiety over things that may never have caused harm. Canada’s radiologists have said plainly that until there is real evidence this improves outcomes, they do not endorse it for average risk adults.

Instead, focus on the screening tests that are actually proven to save lives (but are far less glamorous):
- Mammography for breast cancer
- Colonoscopy or FIT testing for colorectal cancer
- Pap or HPV testing for cervical cancer
- Low dose CT for lung cancer in eligible current or former smokers

These are the cancer screening tests with decades of outcome data behind them. 

Whole body MRIs are used in a very small subset of the population that carry genetic mutations or hereditary syndromes that put them at meaningfully higher risk. For these groups, specialized imaging protocols may be appropriate under a specialist’s guidance.

Thankfully, evidence based screening does not need to be expensive or exotic to work. It needs to be targeted, consistent, and grounded in data.

So, I would save your money until the data is more convincing and the benefit clearly outweighs the harm.

caption:
A tornado warning can be one of the most frightening emergency alerts to receive, but knowing what to do ahead of time can make a real difference.

One of the biggest misconceptions I see is that a tornado watch and a tornado warning mean the same thing. They don’t.

A tornado watch means conditions are favourable for tornadoes to develop. It’s your cue to stay alert, monitor the weather, and make sure you know where you’ll take shelter if needed.

A tornado warning means a tornado has been spotted or detected by weather radar. At that point, don’t wait to look outside or see if it’s coming your way. Go to shelter immediately.

The safest place is a basement. If you don’t have one, move to a small interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building, away from windows and exterior walls. Protect your head and neck, and stay there until officials say it’s safe to come out.

If you’re in a vehicle, your safest option is to get into a sturdy building if you can do so safely. If that’s not possible and a tornado is imminent, leave the vehicle and get as low as possible in a ditch or low-lying area while protecting your head and neck. Despite what many people believe, bridges and overpasses are not safe places to shelter. Winds can actually become stronger as they funnel underneath them, and you’re also exposed to flying debris.

If you live in a mobile home, it’s important to know that even anchored mobile homes are not considered safe during a tornado. If a warning is issued, leave for a sturdy building or designated storm shelter if you have time to do so safely.

Finally, make sure emergency alerts are enabled on your phone and have a plan before severe weather strikes. In an emergency, seconds matter, and having already decided where you’ll go can save valuable time.

Hopefully you’ll never need this information. But if you do, you’ll be glad you knew it.

Save this post so you can find it quickly if severe weather ever heads your way, and share it with someone who lives in a tornado-prone area.

caption:
Doctors aren’t perfect - you won’t ever hear me denying this. 

In particular, we know that women tend to be dismissed by the healthcare system in general, so while the system works to catch up, I want to share a few things you can do to help advocate for yourself. 

1. Document things - both before going in and during a visit, write down symptoms and questions. Take photos or videos - I can’t tell you how valuable these are when patients bring them in. 

2. Bring someone with you - in the stress of requiring emergency care, it can be easy to forget or miss important pieces of information. Bring someone with you who can fill in the blanks and can help remember instructions for afterwards. 

3. Name the concern - it’s human nature to shy away from or dance around the issue you’re worried about. If you’re worried about a heart attack, say it! If you’re worried about cancer, say it. Not only will it help your doctor understand better where you’re coming from, it will help us take pause and think about tests that may need to be done to rule things in or out. 

Always remember that you know your body better than anyone else. Don’t be afraid to advocate for yourself and voice your concerns.

caption:
What does it feel like to live through the climate crisis, not just read about it?

This week gave a clear answer. Wildfire smoke turned the sky orange over Ontario and the Northeast United States, pushing air quality to some of the worst in the world. At the same time, parts of Western Canada are closing in on all time summer rainfall records, with streets flooding and cars stranded in water.

Though many may confuse this for two unrelated weather stories, it’s actually the same crisis showing up in different forms depending on where you live. Rising temperatures are expanding the range of mosquito and tick-borne illness. Milder winters are increasing fungal infections. Deforestation is pushing human populations closer to wildlife and raising the risk of zoonotic disease. Flooding contaminates drinking water. Displacement crowds people into close quarters where disease spreads more easily.

On the other hand, these health impacts are not evenly distributed. People with asthma, older adults, pregnant people, and outdoor workers carry a disproportionate share of the risk from both smoke and flooding.

Of course, this is only the health picture we understand so far. The full scope of the climate crisis is still unfolding.

Sources: Health Canada, Public Health Ontario, Alberta Health Services

If you’re firing up the BBQ this summer, here’s one safety swap worth making: ditch the metal bristle grill brush.

Those tiny wire bristles can break off, stick to the grill and accidentally end up in food. Every year, people end up in the ER with injuries ranging from painful mouth and throat injuries to bowel perforations requiring surgery. It’s uncommon, but when it happens, it can be serious.

A safer alternative? Coil brushes, scraper-style cleaners or even a grill stone. They clean well without the risk of loose metal bristles getting left behind.

If you are still using a wire brush:
• Inspect it regularly for loose or worn bristles
• Replace it often
• Wipe the grill down before cooking
• Consider using a damp cloth or paper towel after brushing to pick up any stray debris

caption:
Multivitamins are one of the most commonly used supplements out there, but the evidence for routine use in otherwise healthy adults is honestly pretty underwhelming.

Large studies have generally not shown meaningful benefits for preventing chronic disease, improving cardiovascular health, reducing cancer risk or helping people live longer. For most people, a multivitamin is not a substitute for sleep, movement, stress management or a balanced diet.

That said, supplements absolutely can play an important role in certain situations, especially when they’re targeted to a specific need or deficiency. Examples include:
* Folic acid in pregnancy or when trying to conceive
* Vitamin D supplementation, particularly in Canada during winter months or in higher-risk groups
* Iron supplementation for iron deficiency
* Vitamin B12 for people with vegan diets or absorption issues
* Calcium/vitamin D in some people at risk for osteoporosis
* Certain gastrointestinal conditions or surgeries that impair nutrient absorption
* Restrictive diets or eating disorders
* Older adults who may be at higher risk of deficiencies

The key point is that “supplements” are not all the same. There’s a big difference between correcting a documented deficiency and taking a generic multivitamin “just in case.”

Also important: more is not always better. Some vitamins and supplements can interact with medications or become harmful at high doses. “Natural” does not automatically mean safe.

If you’re worried you may have a deficiency, it’s worth speaking with your healthcare provider rather than guessing based on social media marketing.

Gum doesn’t sit in your stomach for 7 years. That’s a myth.

Your body can’t digest the gum base, but that doesn’t mean it just stays there. What actually happens is that the rest of the gum (sweeteners, flavouring) gets broken down like any other food, and the gum base moves through your digestive system intact and is passed in your stool, usually within a few days.

So if you accidentally swallow gum, it’s not harmful in typical amounts.

Where we do get concerned:
	•	Repeatedly swallowing large amounts of gum
	•	Especially in kids
	•	Particularly if combined with constipation

In rare cases, that can form a blockage, but this is not common.

Bottom line:
Swallowing gum once in a while is not a problem. It won’t sit in your stomach for years.

If your child has abdominal pain, vomiting, or hasn’t had a bowel movement, that’s when it’s worth getting checked.

Save this for the next time someone brings up the “7-year gum” myth.

caption:
Peptides are everywhere right now, and it’s hard to know what to believe and what not to, so let’s break it all down together. 

“Peptides” aren’t one thing. They’re a broad category of short chains of amino acids. Some are legitimate, evidence-based medications, while Oothers are being marketed far ahead of the science.

The two that come up the most on social media right now are BPC-157 and CJC-1295. Claims related to these 2 peptides include weight loss, injury healing, muscle growth, anti-aging and hormone optimization. 

Unfortunately, the evidence is limited and based largely animal data or very small human studies. There are no large, high-quality randomized controlled trials and no good long-term safety data

There are peptides with strong evidence. For example, GLP-1 receptor agonists used for diabetes and weight loss. But that evidence does not extend to most of the peptides being sold online or through private clinics.

Safety risk also often get downplayed. 

Potential risks include:
- unknown long-term effects
- hormonal disruption, especially through growth hormone and IGF-1 pathways
- fluid retention, joint pain, headaches (reported with GH-related peptides)
- possible impact on glucose metabolism
- injection-related risks (infection, irritation)
- variability in dosing and purity

These products are not approved by Health Canada, so are not subject to the same  to the same quality control as prescription medications. 

Some peptides are powerful, evidence-based tools in medicine.

If you’re considering one, don’t ask “do peptides work?”
Ask: what does the evidence say about this specific peptide?

caption:
Most of the time, when a tooth gets knocked out, it’s either spit out or swallowed (and passes without issue).

But very rarely, it can be aspirated (meaning it goes into the airway instead of the esophagus).

That’s the scenario we worry about.

A tooth sitting in the airway or lung might not cause dramatic symptoms right away. Someone can look relatively well, but over time, it can lead to:
• persistent cough
• recurrent pneumonia
• localized infection or abscess

That’s why if a tooth is missing and unaccounted for after trauma, we don’t just assume it was swallowed. We go looking for it.

A simple chest X-ray can help confirm whether it’s in the airway, and if it is, it needs to be removed.

Bottom line:
If a tooth is knocked out and you can’t find it, don’t ignore it. You need a chest x-ray!

caption:
There is so much information floating around about hormones right now, but not everything trending is actually helpful (or evidence-based).

SKIP OR KEEP: Hormonal Edition

Skip: Hormone tracking kits
Most at-home tests are inconsistent and hard to interpret. Hormones fluctuate a lot day to day, and a single snapshot rarely tells you anything actionable.

Skip: “Hormone balancing” supplements
This isn’t a real medical diagnosis. Many of these are expensive, unregulated, and not backed by good quality evidence.

Keep: Cycle tracking
Understanding your cycle can help you spot patterns, manage symptoms, and know when something’s off. Low risk, high insight.

Skip: Cycle syncing workouts
There’s no strong evidence you need to change your workouts based on your cycle. If it feels good, fine—but it’s not a requirement for “hormone health.” Check out our episode with @drlaurencs1 for more on this. 

Skip: Testosterone pellets
Increasingly marketed to women, often without clear indications or long-term safety data. This isn’t benign.

Keep: Birth control beyond contraception
Birth control isn’t just for preventing pregnancy. It’s used (appropriately) for acne, heavy periods, endometriosis, PCOS, and more—with strong evidence behind it.

Bottom line: hormones are complex. Be wary of anything oversimplified, overpromised, or overpriced.

If something feels off with your cycle or symptoms, that’s worth a real conversation with your doctor—not a quick fix from the internet.

caption:
Casey & Diana is a must see. It plays @citadeltheatreyeg until April 26. 

Set in 1991 at Toronto’s Casey House, during the height of the HIV/AIDS crisis, the story captures a moment in time when fear, stigma and misinformation were shaping not just public opinion, but medical care itself.

While we’ve come a long way in HIV care, stigma in healthcare hasn’t disappeared. I still see it in the assumptions we make, the language we use and the subtle ways patients can feel judged or dismissed. When stigma shows up in healthcare, it doesn’t just hurt feelings, it delays care, erodes trust and ultimately impacts outcomes.

That’s what made this play so powerful.

It doesn’t just tell the story of Princess Diana’s visit, a moment that helped challenge public fear around HIV/AIDS. It centres the humanity of the patients themselves. Their relationships, their humour, their dignity. Their right to be cared for fully, without judgment.

The history behind Casey House makes it even more meaningful.

Opened in 1988, it was Canada’s first stand-alone treatment facility for people living with HIV/AIDS; created at a time when many patients were dying alone, abandoned not just socially but medically. It was founded on a simple but radical idea: that every person deserves compassionate, dignified care. No exceptions.

This play is a reminder, for all of us, that medicine isn’t just about treatment. It’s about how we show up for people, especially when they’re most vulnerable.

Compassion is not optional. Dignity is not conditional.
Stigma has no place in care.

caption:
Thunderclap headache = medical emergency 🚨

This is a headache that comes on suddenly and reaches peak intensity within seconds to minutes. Patients will often describe it as the “worst headache of my life.”

While there are a few possible causes, one of the most serious is a subarachnoid hemorrhage (bleeding in the brain), which can be life-threatening and needs immediate assessment.

What matters most:
• Sudden, explosive onset
• Max intensity right away (within seconds?
• Feels very different from your usual headaches

This is not something to “wait out” or treat at home.

If you or someone else experiences a headache like this, go to the ER immediately or call emergency services.

A few other red flags that should push you to seek urgent care include:
• Neck stiffness
• Vomiting
• Fainting or decreased consciousness
• Neurological symptoms (weakness, vision changes, trouble speaking)
• Headache triggered by exertion, sex, or coughing

Bottom line: when it comes to thunderclap headaches, it’s always better to err on the side of caution.

I’ve been on a string of shifts and have seen some clustered cases of mononucleosis. I thought it would be a good time to give people a refresher on this virus!

Mono is caused by Epstein-Barr virus and can hit hard, especially in teens and young adults.

What people don’t realize:
• The fatigue can last weeks to months
• Sore throat can be severe (often mistaken for strep)
• Your spleen can enlarge which means no contact sports for 6 weeks
• Antibiotics don’t treat it (and some can cause a rash)

What actually helps:
Rest. Hydration. Time.

If you have persistent fever, severe abdominal pain or worsening symptoms, you need to be reassessed.

If you of a family member has had mono, let me know your experience in the comments.

Fevers in kids can feel scary (and a common reason parents bring their kids to the ER) but the approach at home is actually pretty simple.

Here’s how I handle it with my own kids:

1. Don’t chase the number
The temperature matters less than how your child looks and behaves.

2. Treat only if they’re feeling crummy
If they’re uncomfortable, in pain, not drinking or not themselves, that’s when I reach for medication like acetaminophen or ibuprofen. 

3. Watch for red flags
This is the most important part. Fevers are common and usually don’t require a visit to the ER, but there are a few important things to watch for at home. 

When to seek medical care:
* Under 3 months with any fever (38°C/100.4°F or higher)
* Lethargy (difficult to wake or not interacting)
* Trouble breathing
* Signs of dehydration (dry mouth, no tears, peeing much less)
* Severe headache, stiff neck or sensitivity to light
* Persistent vomiting or unable to keep fluids down
* Seizure
* Fever lasting more than 5 days
* Rash that doesn’t blanch or looks like bruising
* You’re worried. Trust that instinct

Bottom line: treat the child, not the number

Save this for the next time your kid spikes a fever because it will happen again

caption:
Gallbladder pain isn’t always obvious, but once you know the pattern, it’s hard to miss.

If you’ve been told you have gallstones or you’re having symptoms that sound like biliary colic (that intense, steady pain in the upper right abdomen, often after eating, sometimes going to your back or shoulder, with nausea), what you eat can make a big difference in how often those attacks happen.

Foods more likely to trigger attacks (try to limit):
- High-fat, greasy or fried foods (deep fried foods, fast food)
- Fatty cuts of meat (bacon, sausage, ribs)
- Full-fat dairy (cream, butter, cheese in large amounts)
- Rich desserts and pastries
- Large, heavy meals

Fat causes your gallbladder to squeeze to release bile. If gallstones are present, that squeeze can trigger pain.

Foods that are generally better tolerated:
- Lean proteins (chicken, turkey, fish, tofu, lentils)
- Low-fat or non-fat dairy
- High-fiber foods (vegetables, fruit, whole grains)
- Smaller, more frequent meals instead of large ones

Diet can help reduce symptoms, but it does NOT get rid of gallstones. If you’re having recurrent attacks, the definitive treatment is surgery to remove the gallbladder.

Go to the ER urgently if you have:
- Pain lasting more than a few hours
- Fever or chills
- Yellowing of your skin or eyes
- Persistent vomiting
- Pain in your chest or shortness of breath

caption:
Colorectal cancer is rising in younger people, and one of the biggest issues we’re seeing is delayed diagnosis.

Partly because symptoms can be subtle.
Partly because they’re easy to explain away.
And partly because we still associate this cancer with “older adults.”

Symptoms you should not ignore:
- Blood in your stool (bright red or dark)
- A persistent change in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or narrower stools)
- Abdominal pain or cramping that doesn’t go away
- Unexplained weight loss
- Fatigue or iron deficiency anemia

If something feels off and persists for more than a few weeks, get it checked

Screening in Canada:
- For average risk, screening typically starts at age 50 (some provinces are moving toward 45)
- Most programs use a stool-based test (FIT) every 1–2 years
- If that test is abnormal → colonoscopy

BUT, you may need earlier and more frequent screening if you have:
- A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer
- A personal history of inflammatory bowel disease
- Genetic syndromes that increase your risk of cancers 

Check your provincial program or talk to your primary care provider about what applies to you.

When to see your doctor (don’t wait for screening age):
- Any of the symptoms above that are persistent or worsening
- Blood in your stool, even once, if it’s unexplained
- New iron deficiency anemia
- Ongoing abdominal symptoms without a clear cause

You do not need to be 50+ to take symptoms seriously. Younger patients are more likely to be diagnosed at later stages, when treatment is more complex. Earlier detection changes outcomes.

If you’re noticing symptoms, don’t self-diagnose or wait it out. Get it checked.

caption:
There are so many claims out there about whole body red light therapy. Recovery. Anti-aging. Sleep. Metabolism. Hair loss. Skin. 

Let’s dig into what the evidence actually says. 

Red light therapy does have some endurance for:
- mild signs of aging in skin
- pattern hair loss 
- some targeted pain conditions

All of the above research is in localized treatment to the specific area, not full body panels. 

Whole body red light panels claim to:
- boost exercise recovery
- increase exercise performance 
- improve sleep
- increase metabolism
- have anti-aging effects on the body

Here’s what the oven actually shows:
1. Exercise, recovery, and performance: systematic review of whole body photobiomodulation found no evidence of benefit.
2. Sleep: possible early signal, but small studies that are not definitive.
3. Inflammation/metabolism: mostly theoretical or based on small, inconsistent studies.
4. Pain: some evidence exist, but primarily for targeted use, not whole body wellness treatments.

So these claims of whole body benefits are really a stretch. Not to mention, these treatments are often expensive, so there’s strong financial incentive to overstate benefits.

Bottom Line: don’t waste your money on whole body Ted light panels 

#redlight #redlighttherapy #metabolichealth #longevity #health

caption:
Toilet seats have an excellent PR team for fear.

But the actual infection risk from sitting on one is extremely low.

Most bacteria and viruses do not survive well on hard, dry surfaces. And intact skin is a very effective barrier. Infections generally require direct contact with mucous membranes, broken skin or transfer via hands.

You cannot get sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia, gonorrhea or HIV from a toilet seat. These organisms do not live long outside the body and require intimate contact for transmission.

UTIs also do not come from toilet seats. They happen when bacteria, usually from your own gut flora, enter the urinary tract. That process does not occur from briefly sitting on a public toilet.

Could bacteria exist on bathroom surfaces? Of course. Bathrooms are not sterile environments. But the more meaningful route of transmission is hand to face, not seat to skin.

Toilet seat covers are mostly about comfort and perception. They are not a game changer for infection prevention.

If you want to reduce risk in public bathrooms:
• Wash your hands well
• Avoid touching your face before hand hygiene
• Teach kids proper handwashing
• Wipe visible contamination if needed

Public health works best when we focus on real risk, not imagined ones.

And in this case, your hands matter a lot more than the seat.

caption:
Gastro season is in full swing in the peds ER right now.

If your house has been hit, here’s what’s typical and what to watch for:

Common symptoms
• Vomiting
• Diarrhea
• Low grade fever
• Crampy abdominal pain
• Fatigue
• Decreased appetite

In kids, vomiting often starts first and can be intense for the first 12 to 24 hours. Diarrhea can follow and last longer.

How long does it last?
• Vomiting: usually 1 to 2 days
• Diarrhea: 3 to 7 days, sometimes up to 10
• Low energy and reduced appetite can linger for several days after

Most cases are viral and self limited.

Management at home
The biggest risk in kids is dehydration.

• Small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution. Think teaspoons every 5 minutes if they can’t tolerate bigger amounts.
• If breastfeeding, continue.
• Avoid forcing large volumes at once.
• Once vomiting improves, reintroduce simple foods as tolerated. No need for a strict “BRAT” diet.
• Focus on fluids over food

You’re looking for:
• Peeing at least every 6 to 8 hours
• Tears when crying
• A moist mouth
• Alertness between episodes

Prevention
• Handwashing with soap and water. This matters more than sanitizer for many viruses.
• Clean high touch surfaces, especially bathrooms.
• Keep kids home from school or daycare until vomiting has stopped for at least 24 hours.

Come to the ER if:
• No urine for 8 hours or more
• Very dry mouth, no tears, sunken eyes
• Lethargy or difficult to wake
• Severe or worsening abdominal pain
• Blood in stool
• Persistent vomiting with inability to keep fluids down
• Signs of dehydration in an infant
• You are worried. Trust your instincts.

Most kids will get through this with supportive care at home. Fluids, patience and time are your best tools.

caption:
Necrotizing fasciitis is rare (I’ve seen it only a handful of times in my 15 year residency and attending career). But when we see it in the ER, it is an all-hands-on-deck situation. 

Necrotizing fasciitis is a deep, aggressive soft tissue infection that involves the layers below the skin. The bacteria release toxins that damage tissue and disrupt blood supply. That loss of blood flow is what allows tissue to die and the infection to move quickly.

It is not bacteria “eating” flesh, but the tissue is dying because of the toxin cutting off blood supply. 

Thankfully, it’s SUPER rare. Roughly 0.4 to 1 per 100,000 people per year in high-income countries. Most skin infections are simple cellulitis and most painful red areas are not necrotizing fasciitis.

Sometimes after a cut, scrape, surgical wound or minor trauma, certain bacteria, like Group A strep, can enter the skin. Sometimes there is no obvious entry point.

Some groups are at higher risk, like those with diabetes, immune compromise, chronic kidney or liver disease, obesity, recent surgery and IV drug use. It can still occur in otherwise healthy people.

Early on it can look unimpressive. The red flag is pain out of proportion to what you see, rapid progression and systemic symptoms. Once sepsis develops, patients can deteriorate quickly.

The bottom line:

If a skin infection is rapidly worsening, severely painful and you feel unwell, that is not something to manage at home

caption:
With a particularly bad influenza season, I’m seeing a lot of this in the pediatric ER right now. 

Your child had a respiratory illness, and just when they were starting to get better, they wake up and refuse to walk because their calves hurt.

That pattern is classic for viral myositis.

This muscle inflammation that can happen during or just after a viral illness. Influenza is the most common trigger, but other viruses can do it too.

Typical symptoms include:
• Sudden calf pain
• Walking on tiptoes or refusing to walk
• Usually both legs
• Otherwise acting normally 

Many parents come in concerned about weakness, but it’s actually pain that is the cause of the child’s refusal to walk. 

Most kids improve within 3 to 7 days with:
• Rest
• Fluids
• Pain control
• Gradual return to activity as tolerated

A rare, but potentially dangerous complication called rhabdomyolysis occurs when muscle breakdown is severe enough to risk kidney injury. Again, this is rare.

Red flags that should prompt reassessment:
• One leg only
• Severe pain out of proportion
• Dark or cola coloured urine
• Persistent high fever or return of fever 
• Dehydration
• True weakness instead of just pain

Has this happened to your child?

caption:
The cold plunge in Lac Beauvert was pure mind over matter.

There’s no easing into it. Your body wants out immediately. Staying becomes an exercise in breath control, focus and choosing calm in discomfort. Somewhere in that space, it turns into meditation.

I’m careful with claims around cold plunges. There isn’t strong evidence that they’re a cure-all or a long-term health intervention. Where the evidence is more consistent is around short-term psychological effects. Brief cold water immersion can increase alertness and temporarily improve mood, largely by forcing present-moment awareness and engaging controlled breathing. You can’t ruminate when every breath matters. 

The benefit isn’t the cold itself so much as voluntary stress, attention and perceived mastery. Paired with heat, it becomes a practice in resilience rather than recovery.

Experiences like this at Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge, especially in a setting like Lac Beauvert, aren’t about biohacking. They’re about presence, perspective and reminding yourself that you can stay steady when things feel uncomfortable.

If you spend enough time online, you’d think longevity depends on a stack of supplements, infusions, hormone optimization, cold exposure, red light panels, biological age tests and some proprietary “protocol.”

That’s the version of longevity that photographs well. It’s also the version people can sell.

The quieter truth is that most of what meaningfully increases lifespan and healthspan is far less glamorous. It’s risk reduction. It’s prevention. It’s consistency over decades.

It’s controlling blood pressure before it causes a stroke.
It’s building muscle before you start losing it.
It’s screening before symptoms show up.
It’s sleeping enough, moving regularly and not smoking.

None of those come with a “link in bio.” None promise dramatic overnight results. And none are especially exciting to post about.

But they work.

Wellness culture often markets optimization. Medicine is still largely about protection.

Longevity isn’t something you hack. It’s something you build slowly, and usually boringly, over time.

3. Manage the walks - make sure snow is cleared and either sand or gravel are put down to help increase grip on icy sidewalks.

caption:
Post-viral coughs can be frustrating. You feel “better,” but the cough just hangs on. This is common. After a viral respiratory infection, airway inflammation and heightened cough reflexes can persist for weeks, sometimes up to 6 to 8 weeks, even when the infection itself has resolved.

A few simple, evidence-informed strategies that can help calm things down:

• Warm fluids
Tea, broth, warm water with lemon. These help keep secretions thin, soothe irritated airways, and can reduce that dry, tickly cough sensation.

• Humidifier at night
Dry air can worsen airway irritation and coughing, especially overnight. Adding moisture to the air may reduce throat dryness and improve sleep quality.

• Nasal saline
Post-nasal drip is a major driver of lingering coughs. Saline sprays or rinses help clear mucus, reduce nasal irritation, and limit that constant throat clearing.

• Honey
Honey has been shown to reduce cough frequency and severity, particularly at night. A spoonful before bed or mixed into warm tea can help coat and soothe the throat. Not for children under 1 year.

If a cough is worsening, associated with shortness of breath, chest pain, fevers that return, coughing up blood, or lasting beyond 8 weeks, it’s time to check in with a healthcare provider. But for many people, patience plus supportive care is the fix.

Save this for the next time a “simple virus” overstays its welcome.

caption:
When your kid is vomiting, it’s stressful and exhausting, but a few key principles can really help.

Most childhood gastro is viral, and while it can look dramatic, it’s usually short-lived, often improving over 24–72 hours.

1) Fluids matter more than food
It’s completely normal for kids to have no appetite. Don’t force eating. The goal is hydration. Offer small, frequent sips every 5–10 minutes. Oral rehydration solutions are ideal, but diluted juice, popsicles, or clear fluids can work if that’s all they’ll take.

2) Watch urine output
Hydration is better measured by peeing than by how much they drink. Aim for at least 3–4 pees or wet diapers in 24 hours. Fewer than that, very dark urine, a dry mouth, or lethargy are red flags.

3) Use anti-nausea medication when needed
Anti-nauseants don’t cure gastro, but they can reduce vomiting enough to help kids keep fluids down and lower the risk of dehydration.

When to go to the ER:
• Signs of dehydration (very low urine output, dry mouth, no tears, sunken eyes)
• Persistent vomiting that won’t stop despite small sips or medication
• Blood or bright green fluid in vomit
• Severe belly pain, a hard or very tender abdomen
• Lethargy, confusion, or your child is hard to wake
• Infants under 6 months, or anytime your gut says something isn’t right

A few other things to know:
• Diarrhea often lasts longer than vomiting and can linger for several days.
• Handwashing with soap and water is key. Many gastro viruses don’t respond well to hand sanitizer.
• Keep kids home while actively vomiting and for at least 24 hours after it stops, when possible.

If you’re worried, trust your instincts. That’s always a good enough reason to get your child checked.

caption:
Keep or Skip: Cough & Cold Remedies (What the Evidence Actually Says)

There’s no shortage of home remedies for coughs and colds, but not all of them hold up when you look at the data.

SKIP
• Steam inhalation – Feels soothing, but studies don’t show it shortens illness or improves outcomes. There’s also a real burn risk, especially for kids.
• Zinc lozenges – Evidence is mixed at best, benefit (if any) is small, and side effects like nausea and bad taste are common.
• Echinacea – Large reviews show no consistent benefit for preventing or treating colds.
• Homeopathic cough syrups – No active ingredient, no biologically plausible mechanism, no evidence beyond placebo.
• Onions on the feet – This is a myth. Colds are caused by viruses, not toxins being “pulled out.”

KEEP
• Humidifier – Adding moisture to dry air can reduce throat irritation and make coughing more tolerable, especially overnight.
• Vitamin D – Modest evidence suggests adequate vitamin D levels may reduce respiratory infection risk, particularly in people who are deficient.
• Honey for cough (over age 1) – Strong evidence that honey reduces cough frequency and severity, especially at night.

Bottom line: comfort matters, but evidence matters more. If a remedy is harmless and helps symptoms, great. If it’s ineffective, risky, or just expensive placebo, it’s okay to skip it.

caption:
Fevers in kids can be scary! Rest assured that fevers, themselves, are not dangerous and are actually a good thing. 

What matters more than the number on the thermometer is the context.

I always say, “Treat the child, not the number.” 
Comfort, fluids and observation matter more than forcing the fever down. If your child is running around and happy but happens to have a fever, there’s no need to treat it. If they’re clingy, look uncomfortable, not drinking well and look miserable, definitely treat. We don’t want our kids suffering. 

A fever should be medically assessed if:
• Your child is under 3 months old with any fever (≥38°C / 100.4°F)
• The fever lasts more than 4-5 days
• Your child looks unwell, lethargic or is difficult to wake
• There is trouble breathing, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration
• Your child has a seizure, stiff neck or severe headache
• You are worried or something feels off as a parent

Be sure to follow me @drshazmamithani for more helpful help tips for all ages and share this with your friends and family.

The hospitals are busy and people are looking for care around this time of year. Remember that the ER isn’t the only option.

• Family doctor same-day appointments – many clinics hold urgent same-day spots. Most people don’t realize this exists, but it’s worth calling and asking.

• Urgent care centres – for things that can’t wait but aren’t life-threatening.
• Health Link (811) – a great first step if you’re unsure where to go.
• Education – knowing what’s safe to manage at home matters. That’s why I share evidence-based guidance here.

And to be very clear:
If it’s an emergency, if symptoms are severe, or if you’re worried or unsure — go to the ER. We are always there for you.

KEEP or SKIP: Sleep Edition

If you’ve ever gone down a sleep-hacks rabbit hole, you’re not alone. There’s no shortage of advice online, but not all of it is backed by evidence and some of it can actually make sleep worse.

Magnesium – KEEP
Magnesium can help with sleep quality and muscle relaxation, especially in people who are deficient. It is not a sedative, but for some, it can be a helpful part of a nighttime routine.

Melatonin – IT DEPENDS 
Melatonin works best for circadian rhythm issues like jet lag, shift work, or delayed sleep phase. It is not meant to be a long-term, nightly sleep aid, and more is not better. Dose and timing matter.

Sleep trackers – KEEP (with boundaries)
Trackers can be useful for spotting trends and patterns over time. If the data starts to cause stress or anxiety about “perfect sleep,” it can become counterproductive.

Blue light glasses – SPLIT DECISION
Sheila keeps them. Shaz skips them. The evidence is mixed. Reducing screen time, dimming lights, and having a consistent bedtime routine likely matter more.

Weighted blankets – KEEP
For some people, especially those with anxiety, weighted blankets can help with relaxation and falling asleep. If it feels calming and safe, that benefit counts.

Alcohol before bed – SKIP
Alcohol may help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep and reduces overall sleep quality. You wake up less rested, even if you slept longer.

Exercise late at night – SKIP
Intense exercise close to bedtime can make it harder to fall asleep for many people. Earlier in the day or early evening is usually better.

Mouth taping – SKIP
There is limited evidence and real safety concerns. It is not a treatment for snoring or sleep apnea. Ongoing fatigue or loud snoring should be medically assessed.

Sleep is not one-size-fits-all, but good sleep advice should be evidence-based.

If you’ve seen vibration plates marketed as a shortcut for metabolism, fat loss, detox, or “lymphatic drainage,” the evidence simply doesn’t support those claims. These devices have been pushed hard in the wellness space, but high-quality research just isn’t there.

What we do see are small, inconsistent studies showing potential benefits for specific groups, like older adults working on balance, or modest improvements in bone mineral density when vibration is combined with other exercises. There’s also some early research on reduced muscle soreness after workouts, but again, nothing strong or consistent.

It’s also important to note that these devices aren’t appropriate for everyone. People who are pregnant, have implanted devices such as pacemakers, have active deep-vein thrombosis, unstable cardiovascular disease, recent fractures or joint replacements, severe osteoporosis, or significant vestibular disorders should avoid vibration platforms or use them only under clinical guidance. For these groups, the potential risks outweigh any of the uncertain benefits.

For most people, especially if you’re already active, these machines don’t replace the fundamentals that truly move the needle for health: strength training, regular cardio, and daily movement.

KEEP or SKIP: Supplements Edition
We get asked all the time which supplements are actually worth it. Here’s what the evidence says

FIBRE - KEEP
Most of us fall short on daily fibre. It supports gut health, lowers cholesterol, improves blood sugar control, and may even reduce colorectal cancer risk. Ideally, get it from food, but if you can’t hit 25–30 g/day, a psyllium or inulin supplement can help.
Evidence: Anderson et al., Nutr Rev. 2009;77(4):188–205.

MULTIVITAMINS - SKIP
For most healthy adults, they don’t prevent chronic disease or extend lifespan. Unless you have a specific deficiency, extra vitamins just make for expensive urine.
Evidence: Fortmann et al., Ann Intern Med. 2013;159(12):824–834.

DETOXES - SKIP
There’s no evidence that detox teas, juices, or cleanses eliminate toxins. Your liver and kidneys do that 24/7. Some detox products can actually be harmful or cause electrolyte imbalances.
Evidence: Ernst E. J Hum Nutr Diet. 2012;25(6):505–512.

VITAMIN D - KEEP
In northern climates, most of us don’t get enough year-round sunlight. Supplementation (especially in fall/winter) supports bone and immune health.
Evidence: Holick MF, N Engl J Med. 2007;357:266–281.

CREATINE - CONDITIONAL KEEP
Creatine is one of the most researched and effective supplements, but its benefits show up only if you’re doing consistent strength or resistance training. It can improve muscle strength, exercise recovery, and lean mass. For non–strength trainers, there’s little proven benefit yet (though early research hints at possible cognitive and bone perks).
Evidence: Kreider et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:18; Devries & Phillips, Nutrients. 2014;6(1):31–47.

caption:
Not all bugs need drugs!

Many of the illnesses that most people assume need antibiotics - like sore throats, coughs and ear infections - are actually caused by viruses, meaning that antibiotics don’t effectively treat them. 

There are some infections - like urinary tract and skin infections - where antibiotics would be the first line choice, because these are usually bacterial. 

Could a sore throat, cough or ear infection be bacterial? Absolutely, more information is needed before antibiotics are prescribed. This includes a throat swab (for strep throat), physical exam findings or a chest x-ray (for pneumonia) and more time (for an ear infection). 

Antibiotics are not without risk and they’re not specific just to the bacteria causing an infection. They can wipe out the good bacteria that live in and on your body, which help maintain overall health. 

So, next time you are prescribed antibiotics by your doctor or pharmacist, be sure to stop and ask exactly why they’re being prescribed and whether further testing or time is needed.

Oral collagen has become a big wellness trend — but what does the evidence actually say?

The research isn’t perfect (most studies are small and industry-funded), but so far it suggests potential benefits:
- Modest improvements in skin hydration, elasticity, and wrinkle depth
- Some evidence for joint pain relief in osteoarthritis and athletes
- Possible support for nail and hair strength

Importantly, collagen supplements are generally considered safe with minimal side effects, which is why I recently started using one myself. I figure, with little harm and some potential benefit, it’s worth a try. 

Bottom line: The science isn’t definitive, but collagen may offer small benefits — and given the low risk, it’s reasonable if you’re interested. Just don’t expect a miracle in a jar.

• A randomized trial (PMID 30122200) found improved skin elasticity and joint comfort after 90 days.
• A systematic review (PMID 30681787) highlights consistent gains in skin hydration, elasticity, and collagen density, with no reported side effects.
• Another study (PMID 39021368) boosted skin hydration by ~14%, elasticity by ~23%, and reduced wrinkle depth by ~20% in just 12 weeks.

caption:
I have some bad news…hand foot mouth disease season is here. HFMD is caused by a viral infection that tends to be most common in the late summer and early fall. It’s not unusual for us to start seeing cases as school starts up again, and kids are sharing germs. 

The most common virus causing HFMD is coxsackie virus. There are other viruses that can cause it as well. It is spread from person to person by respiratory droplets (sneezing, coughing, saliva) and poop, so hand washing is the most important way to stop spread. Because it is viral, antibiotics are not needed, and do not work. 

Although HFMD is most common in the summer and fall, it’s not unusual to see outbreaks throughout the year, especially as the weather warms up in the spring. 

Both children and adults can get HFMD, and symptoms tend to be more severe in adults. The best way to prevent spread is to stay home when sick and wash your hands!

Symptoms are usually supportive and include keeping up with fluids and treating pain and fever with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Creams and ointments are not effective. 

It’s important to see a doctor if any of the following things occur:
- if there are concerns about dehydration because of decreased fluid intake 
- if there is a fever for more than 5 days
- if any of the skin lesions start getting increasing redness around them 
- if you or your child are unwell, not drinking, not acting themselves or confused, lightheaded or passing out, or of course, if you’re worried 

People can be contagious for upto a week after symptoms start, so don’t return to daycare, school, or work until all of the lesions are gone. 

Make sure to follow, share, and save!

Have you heard that mosquitoes might have a blood type preference?!

A study done in 2004 showed that, compared to type A blood type, mosquitoes are more likely to land on someone with blood type O. Another study done in 2019 showed that mosquitoes prefer feeding on blood type O blood when presented with all blood type options in feeders (so not actual humans). This certainly isn’t definitive, but may indicate that mosquitoes have a preference toward blood type O. 

That being said, there are several other factors that likely have a much bigger impact on how much mosquitoes are attracted to you. 

1. Your scent - certain chemical in your sweat can attract mosquitoes, so perhaps showering post workout is beneficial in more ways than one!
2. The amount of CO2 in your breath - mosquitoes are attracted to CO2, and sometimes (like in pregnancy) the amount you breathe out can be higher.
3. Dark Clothing - mosquitoes tend to be attracted to darker clothing. 
4. Body Heat - mosquitoes can sense heat and are attracted to it. 

Here are some important ways to help protect you from mosquitoes:
1. Wear long sleeves and pants 
2. Avoid being out at dusk/dawn
3. Wear an insect repellent containing DEET or other CDC recommended repellents 
4. Permethrin treated clothing

caption:
Time for another Keep or Skip - The skincare edition. Here’s what the evidence says about five popular products and tools:

Sunscreen
A strong keep. Regular daily use reduces photoaging, hyperpigmentation, and skin cancer risk. Broad-spectrum SPF 30+ is recommended by every major dermatology society, and consistent use outperforms virtually any other topical in long-term skin health.

Retinoids
Another clear keep. The best evidence we have for improving fine lines, pigmentation, and skin texture. Retinoids increase cell turnover, stimulate collagen production, and are a cornerstone of evidence-based skincare. Prescription forms are strongest, but OTC retinol also has supportive data.

Vitamin C serum
A keep. L-ascorbic acid is one of the most studied antioxidants in skincare. It helps reduce oxidative stress from UV and pollution, improves brightness, and supports collagen synthesis. Formulation matters: it must be stabilized and ideally paired with vitamin E and ferulic acid.

Red light masks
A cautious keep. There’s growing evidence that low-level light therapy can improve fine lines, redness, and inflammation by stimulating cellular energy pathways. But results are modest, devices vary widely in quality, and evidence is still emerging. Best used as an adjunct—not a replacement for foundational skincare.

Collagen supplements
We split here. Shaz keeps, Sheila skips. Some small studies suggest potential benefits for skin hydration and elasticity, but evidence is limited and often industry-funded. Collagen peptides are generally safe, but results vary and whole-food protein remains a proven alternative. A possible add-on, not a must-have.

Bottom line: Sunscreen and retinoids remain the strongest evidence-based anchors in skincare. Vitamin C and red light therapy offer additional, modest benefits. Collagen supplements are optional—and the science is still catching up.

caption:
Blood clots are a risk during travel that everyone should know about. 

A blood clot in the leg is called a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Travel by land or plane slightly increases the risk of DVT, especially if the travel time is more than 4 hours. 

In otherwise healthy people, the increased risk is much less than 1%, but this risk can be higher for people with:
- recent major surgery 
- previous blood clots
- cancer
- pregnancy
- obesity
- taking an estrogen containing medication 
- blood clotting disorder 

If you have any of these risk factors, it’s important to talk to your doctor about whether you should take any medications to prevent a DVT while traveling. 

In general, here are a few things everyone can do to help decrease the risk of DVT:
- wear compression stockings
- getting up to walk every 1-2 hours
- flex and extend your ankles and knees frequently (the muscle movement helps keep the blood moving in your leg veins)
- staying we hydrated 
- avoid alcohol 

The risk of travel-related DVT is highest in the first 2 weeks, so it’s important to see a doctor if you think you may have one. Signs of DVT include pain, swelling, or redness to your calf or thigh. 

Blood clots can dislodge from the leg and travel to your lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism (PE), which can be a medical emergency. Symptoms of PE include chest pain, shortness of breath, racing heart, lightheadedness/dizziness, or passing out. If you think you have a PE, go to the ER right away.

The wasps have re-emerged over the last couple weeks in #yeg and beyond. 

When wasps sting, most of the time they cause a small local reaction (pain, redness, swelling and itching). The symptoms can increase over a few hours and then tend to resolve over 2-3 days. 

Some people can get what’s called a large local reaction, where the swelling and redness continues to worsen for several days before resolving after about a week. This is a common reason people come to the ER, but this is usually not a big deal and just takes symptoms control and time. 

Even more rare is an anaphylactic reaction to wasps, which can include a generalized rash (hives), airway/mouth/lip swelling, breathing difficult, low blood pressure and vomiting. This is a medical emergency that requires an EpiPen and getting to the ER right away. This is not what I’m discussing here today. 

Any wasp sting is also at risk for a secondary bacterial infection, so if you notice increasing redness, pain or fever, you need to see a doctor for antibiotics. 

Here are some tips for kids and adults who are unlucky enough to be stung. These can be used for other stings like yellow jackets, bees, and hornets too. Just be sure to look for a stinger and remove it. 

The best way to manage pain is to use cool compresses or ice and anti inflammatory medications like ibuprofen (as long as it’s safe for you to take). 

The best way to manage itching is cool compresses and antihistamines (as long as it’s safe for you to take) if the itching is immediate. For delayed itching, topical steroids like hydrocortisone can be used (as long as it’s safe for you to use it). This would be a good medication to have a discussion with your pharmacist about.

caption:
Are you a parent worried about measles exposure in your baby?

With measles cases on the rise in North America, I’ve been getting a lot of questions about how best to protect you young babies who are too young to get their MMR vaccine. 

First, rest assured that your baby will get some protection from the immune birthing (through antibodies that cross the placenta) and breastfeeding parent(s) (through antibodies in breastmilk). Though this protection isn’t perfect, it’s better than nothing. 

Measles is a highly contagious, airborne virus. It’s one of the most contagious diseases known and can actually stay in the air for hours after an infectious person leaves it. 2 MMR doses offer 97% protection from the disease and the first dose is typically recommended at 1 year of age. 

Here are precautions I recommend for those with babies too young to get vaccinated for measles:
1. Limit times indoors with people outside your family, especially crowded public indoor spaces .
2. Be upfront and ask your friends and family about their vaccination status before any visits. It’s not about judgement, it’s about protecting your little one who doesn’t have a fully developed immune system yet and is in a high risk category with measles. If you’re unsure, opt to spend time outdoors at a distance and forego any snuggles or contact. 
3. Ask your local public health office about whether your baby is eligible for a 6 month MMR vaccine. Usually, the first dose is at 12 months and the second dose is between 18 months and 4 years. If your baby does get an early dose, they will still require the 2 standard timed doses as well. 

Leave any questions in the comments and be sure to share with any friends that have new babies.

caption:
How do you identify misinformation online?

For me, there are 3 key questions:

1. Who is giving you the information? 
Are they a regulated health professional (I.e. do they have a college or regulatory body that they are accountable to)? This is important because regulated professionals have a professional code of conduct that they must follow. They can’t just say false things without consequences. 

Some examples of regulated health professionals include doctors, nurses, dieticians, physiotherapists, pharmacists and optometrists. 

2. Are they trying to sell you something?
A lot of disinformation is linked to the supplement industry, which is worth over 4 times that of the pharmaceutical industry. If the person you’re watching is speaking about a specific product that helped them, and then are recommending you buy that product, take immediate pause. When someone financially benefits from a product (like a cleanse/detox, supplement, etc) there is inherent bias in the information they’re sharing. Approach with caution. 

3. Does it sound too good to be true?
If it does, it probably is. In the age of quick fixes, we all want something that will be a one stop shop solution for our health concerns. Unfortunately, health is complex and multifactorial. 

What else do you look at when deciding what health information or creator to follow? Let me know in the comments.

caption:
The weather is warming up, which means more time in and around water. 

Drowning is one of the scariest things that goes through my brain when my kids are near water, both as a mom and an ER doctor. According to @cdcgov children aged 1-4 are more likely to die from drowning than any other cause. Drowning is often quick, and unlike what you see on TV, it’s often silent. Any one of any age is at risk of drowning when near water. 

The good news is that drowning can be prevented with some simple and practical tips. 

Swimming lessons can reduce the risk of drowning, but that doesn’t mean that supervision isn’t needed. It’s so important to always supervise closely. Have a designated, sober adult who is in charge of constantly watching people in the water. The designated supervisor should not be doing any other activities that could distract them like chatting, reading, using a device or consuming any substances. All substances should be avoided for swimmers too, as consuming substances and swimming increases drowning risk significantly. 

Supervision doesn’t stop at pools and natural bodies of water. Bathtubs also pose a significant drowning risk. Make sure wells or other water containers are covered with a lid to prevent accidental falls into them. 

For little swimmers who don’t have strong swimming skills and for every person on a boat, life jackets can save lives. Life jackets in pools do not mean that constant supervision still isn’t needed. Also, air-filled floaties don’t count!

If you have a pool at home, make sure you have a fence that is at least 4 feet high and fully encloses the pool. It should have self-closing and latching gates. 

CPR skills can be life saving in situations beyond just drowning. If you need a suggestion on a local organization that provides basic life support training, send me a DM and I can help you find something. 

Please share this with friends and family - you could save a life ❤️

As an ER Doctor and Mom of 2 kids, one of my (probably) irrational fears is around kids and cars. 

I’ve seen enough vehicles injure young kids to be sure to extra diligent on walks and in parking lots. Not only are kids often too short to see over the hood of a vehicle, they are also more likely to dart out into a street without warning. 

From a young age, my husband and I started playing red light green light with our kids while out on walks in the neighborhood. While we made sure it was fun for the kids, we also continued to emphasize the importance of immediately stopping when RED LIGHT is called. 

This has been a great tool for us as we’ve continued neighborhood walks, city walks, and even indoor walks in busy places. 

When things are particularly busy or high traffic, the additional rule is that each kid has to hold hands with an adult as well until things are safer.

caption:
October is Breast Cancer Awareness month, but breast health is something we need to think about year round. 

It’s important to understand the importance of screening for breast cancer, how screening is done and when to start. All of the information in this post pertains to people who are NOT high risk. Anyone high risk should talk to their doctor about the right timing and type(s) of screening, as the general rules outlined here don’t apply. 

There has been a lot of discussion around what age is best to start screening for breast cancer. Breast cancer screening should absolutely start by age 50, but there is growing evidence and guidelines that support starting earlier at 40. 

The most important takeaway here is that starting screening at 40 comes with some additional risks (like overdiagnosis, increased biopsies, increased patient anxiety and more). This is why it’s SO important to talk to your health care provider about the pros and cons of starting in your 40s. 

Depending on where you live, you can self refer for mammograms starting at age 40. If you live in a province that doesn’t allow this, you’ll need a referral.

caption:
In preparation for our upcoming start of season 2 of The Doc Talk, we put together a series of “Keep or Skip.”

Let’s dig into the evidence on 5 wellness trends:

Weighted vests – Limited evidence for benefit. If you’re spending time or money, invest it in regular weight training instead for stronger gains in muscle, bone, and overall health.

Strength training – Strong evidence to KEEP. Improves muscle mass, bone density, metabolic health, and reduces risk of chronic disease. Recommended at least 2x/week for all adults.

Walking for cardio – Definite KEEP. Regular brisk walking lowers cardiovascular risk, supports mental health, and is a sustainable form of aerobic activity across the lifespan.

Cold plunges – Mixed evidence. Some short-term studies suggest improvements in mood, alertness, and reduced muscle soreness. But data on long-term health benefits is limited, and risks include cold shock and arrhythmias in people with heart conditions. (Shazma keeps, Sheila skips.)

Alcohol for sleep – Clear SKIP. Alcohol may shorten sleep onset but disrupts sleep architecture, decreases REM sleep, and worsens overall sleep quality and next-day function.

Takeaway: The strongest evidence supports strength training and walking as core health habits. Cold plunges are interesting but not essential, and alcohol remains harmful for sleep health.

👉 Which of these are part of your routine?

Save and share to your stories. This is going to be a hot week across the country, meaning a significantly increased risk of heat stroke. 

Heat Stroke is a life threatening illness that can progress very rapidly if you’re not doing things to protect yourself. 

Here are important things to keep in mind to avoid heat illness and heat stroke:
🥵 Avoid exercise outdoors, especially from 11-4, and try to exercise early in the morning or indoors. Exertion in the heat is one of the biggest risk factors for heat stroke. 
🥵Wear light coloured and loose clothing. Tight clothes make it more difficult for sweat to help cool you down. When sweat evaporates from the skin, it helps cool the body down. Looser clothing will also allow airflow for better evaporation and cooling. 
🥵Stay well hydrated - sweat is an important way that the body cools down in the heat, and staying hydrated helps with normal sweat production. Avoid alcohol, as this acts as a diuretic (makes you pee more) and will dehydrate you. 
🥵Take breaks in the shade and indoors to help cool down. 
🥵 Use cool compresses or mist water to help with cooling by evaporation from the skin, as well as from applying cold to the skin. Adding a fan will help with cooling as well. 

Make sure to follow for more helpful health content and share with your friends and family work to keep them safe too.
